title: Pressure-cooker yoghurt
subtitle: Thick, live-culture yoghurt with no specialist equipment
excerpt: Homemade yoghurt made in the pressure cooker using the keep-warm function for incubation. The result is thick, tangy, and live, better than most shop-bought equivalents and considerably cheaper.
sourceNotes: Yoghurt has been made at home across South Asian, Middle Eastern, and Eastern European cooking for thousands of years. The process, heat milk, cool, inoculate with live culture, incubate, is identical in every tradition. The electric pressure cooker popularised using the pressure cooker for incubation in the 2010s.

recipe.batchNotes: Use the previous batch as the starter for the next, reserve 2 tablespoons from each batch.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Yoghurt keeps refrigerated for up to 2 weeks.
recipe.temperatureNote: Incubation temperature. Milk must be cooled to 43°C before the starter is added.

content.text: The pressure cooker does two things in this recipe. First, it heats the milk to pasteurisation temperature. Then it holds the milk warm while the culture sets. A thermometer is the only tool needed. The starter goes in at around 43°C, and that temperature is the one critical step.

The starter is a few tablespoons of plain live yoghurt containing active cultures. The culture converts the milk sugars into lactic acid over 8 to 10 hours, setting the milk into yoghurt. After the first batch, reserve a small amount to start the next one.

For thicker yoghurt, strain the finished batch through a muslin cloth in the fridge for 2 to 4 hours. This removes whey and produces a Greek-style consistency. The strained whey is useful in baking and smoothies.

Pour {{whole-milk}} of whole milk into the pressure cooker. Select the sauté or heat function (or use it on the hob) and bring the milk to 85°C, stirring occasionally to prevent scorching on the base. Do not boil. Once 85°C is reached, turn off the heat and allow the milk to cool to 43°C, this takes about 20 to 30 minutes. A thermometer is essential here.

Once the milk is at exactly 43°C, add the 2 tablespoons of plain live yoghurt. Whisk gently to combine. The temperature must be between 38°C and 46°C, too cool and the culture will not activate; too hot and it will be killed.

Set the pressure cooker to its keep-warm function (do not seal the lid under pressure). Incubate at keep-warm for 8 hours, overnight is convenient. Do not disturb the pot during this time. After 8 hours, the yoghurt should have set. It will look thick and slightly wobbly. Refrigerate immediately for at least 4 hours before eating to firm it further.

rows.symptom: The yoghurt has not set after 8 hours
rows.cause: The milk was too hot when the starter was added, killing the culture; or the keep-warm temperature is too low.
rows.fix: Check the yoghurt starter packaging confirms live cultures. If the milk was above 46°C when inoculated, the culture was likely killed, start again with a fresh starter. Incubate for a further 2 hours if the pot temperature was the issue.

rows.cause: Skimmed or semi-skimmed milk was used instead of whole milk, or incubation was insufficient.
rows.fix: Use whole milk for the best set. To thicken, strain through muslin in the fridge for 2 to 4 hours.

rows.cause: Over-incubation, left for longer than 10 hours at keep-warm temperature.
rows.fix: Taste after 8 hours. The longer the incubation, the more sour the result. Stop at 8 hours for a mild yoghurt, 10 hours for tangier.

content.text: Home-made yoghurt is a habit once established. The cost is a litre of milk and a couple of tablespoons of the previous batch, a fraction of shop-bought Greek yoghurt. It suits a household that eats yoghurt regularly at breakfast, in dips, as a sauce for curries, or in baking. The pressure cooker makes both the heating and incubation phases straightforward without specialist yoghurt-making equipment.
